blocks.title: Logistic regression
blocks.text: Logistic regression predicts an outcome that is yes or no. Instead of an exact number, it gives a probability between 0 and 1: P = 1 / (1 + e^-(b0 + b1 x)), where e is the base of natural logarithms, b0 the intercept (log-odds when x = 0) and b1 how much the log-odds change per unit of x.

A predicted probability of 0.85 means an 85% chance of passing. The book supposes b0 = 1 and b1 = 0.6. With these values, 5 hours gives P = 1 / (1 + e^-4), about 0.98, and 4 hours gives 1 / (1 + e^-3.4), about 0.97. The book prints 0.83 and 0.73, which are the values for 1 hour and 0 hours. These assumed coefficients also do not fit the data, since they predict passing even for students who studied 1 hour and failed. A model fitted to this data would have a negative intercept, so its probability crosses 0.5 between 3 and 4 hours.

blocks.long_description: The fruit-stall data lie exactly on the line earnings = 100 + 40 x customers, so 22 customers predict 980 rupees, and on day 6 the model predicted 1,220 for 28 customers against an actual 1,250. A logistic model turns study hours into a probability of passing that rises in an S-shape from near 0 to near 1, crossing 0.5 between the failing and passing students; the curve drawn is illustrative. K-means with K = 2 groups Basim, Umer and Maliha around a centre at Math 78.3, English 65, and Anie and Tallat around Math 45, English 82.5. A model is built by defining the problem, collecting data, choosing an algorithm, training and evaluating on new data.

blocks.prompt: How does logistic regression differ from linear regression?
blocks.explanation: Linear regression predicts a number on a straight line; logistic regression predicts the probability (0 to 1) of a yes-or-no outcome along an S-shaped curve.

items: Logistic regression: P = 1 / (1 + e^-(b0 + b1 x)) gives a pass probability between 0 and 1.
